pull.title: headersync: do parameter search at runtime
pull.body:
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime during startup. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.

`ComputeHeadersSyncParams()` doesn't terminate for a small `minchainwork_headers`
combined with a short timespan:

```c++
ComputeHeadersSyncParams(std::chrono::seconds{0}, 30228);  // hangs
ComputeHeadersSyncParams(std::chrono::seconds{0}, 30229);  // period=2 bufsize=40
```

30229 is the boundary; below it the region extends out to timespans around 1e4 s.

In `attack_rate()`, the left side of `future_limit * prob < 1.0e-16 * rate` can't be
negative, and the right side is exactly 0 once `rate` is below ~2.5e-308, so that
break stops being reachable. The `limit` check is the only other exit and Step 1's
Newton call doesn't pass one, so there it has none at all.

The Python this replaces has the same shape
(`HEADER_BATCH_COUNT * prob < 1.0e-16 * rate * len(align_choices)`) and doesn't
terminate at those arguments either, so it isn't new, it just matters more now that
it runs at startup.

Non-strict is enough, since `prob` decreases to exactly 0 and takes the left side
with it:

```c++
-    if (future_limit * prob < 1.0e-16 * rate) break;
+    if (future_limit * prob <= 1.0e-16 * rate) break;
```

are unchanged.

headerssync: add computation of optimal sync parameters

Add ComputeHeadersSyncParams(), which finds (near-)optimal commitment
period and redownload buffer size values for the headers sync
DoS-protection mechanism, given the timespan since genesis and the
number of headers in the minimum-chainwork chain, along with the
internal ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner() it is based on.

The attack model treats headers as arriving one at a time, which
slightly overestimates what an attacker can achieve (in reality headers
arrive in batches that are only accepted in their entirety), but leads
to a closed-form expression for the expected number of accepted forged
headers. The optimization problem is then solved by bisecting for the
largest integer period below the optimum of its continuous relaxation,
and comparing that period with the next one.

The unit test checks 50 inputs against their exact optima, found by an
exhaustive search over all periods.

fuzz: add headers sync parameter computation targets

Add two fuzz targets covering the headers sync parameter optimizer over
the entire range of legal inputs, asserting that the resulting
configuration is sane (and, implicitly, that the computation terminates
without crashing or throwing):

- headers_sync_params_inner exercises ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner
  directly. minchainwork_headers is a block height and thus fits an int;
  max_headers must exceed twice that (which the caller guarantees by
  clamping) and is at most 6 headers/s over the longest timespan that
  std::chrono::seconds is guaranteed to represent; attack_headers is any
  positive rate, parametrized logarithmically.

- headers_sync_params exercises ComputeHeadersSyncParams with any
  representable timespan, and any int-height minchainwork_headers.

Both targets check that the returned period is positive and no larger
than the minimum-chainwork chain, and that the redownload buffer covers
at least one commitment period whenever the acceptable attack rate is
low enough to require any commitment verification at all (which it
always is for the rates ComputeHeadersSyncParams uses).

net_processing: compute headers sync parameters at runtime

So far, the headers sync parameters are committed to the repository,
as part of the chain parameters. This requires maintainers to
occasionally recompute them, based on a prediction of how long the
release is likely to be used.

With the optimization algorithm now available in headerssync.cpp, it
becomes possible to instead do this computation at runtime. This is
less work, with fewer ways for maintainers and reviewers to get it
wrong, and automatically adjusts based on clock time.

The computation takes well under a microsecond, so even tests and fuzz
targets which construct a PeerManager per iteration can simply do it
every time. Those fuzz targets already fix the clock before construction,
so the parameters they end up with do not vary with the fuzz input.

As the chain parameters no longer hold them, HeadersSyncParams moves to
headerssync.h, next to the code which computes and consumes it.

Co-Authored-By: Lőrinc <pap.lorinc@gmail.com>

contrib: remove headerssync-params.py

The headers sync parameters are now computed at runtime, so the tool
that used to generate them for chainparams.cpp has no purpose anymore.

test: verify the sync parameters by brute force

The existing vectors compare against values obtained by a separate
exhaustive search, so they detect changes in behavior, but not a mistake
in that search. Add a test which establishes from scratch that the
returned configuration really is the one with the lowest memory usage,
by evaluating the attack rate for every integer period, and for every
integer bufsize up to the point where it becomes acceptable.

To make this possible, the attack rate computation becomes a function
rather than a lambda inside ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner().

comments.body: Is there any anonymity breaking via `NodeClock::now()` influencing these parameters? (I think maybe not, but might be worth quantizing or similar to guarantee it?)

Good point, I had not considered that.

The choice of the commitment period should not be observable (besides a very minor time leak perhaps). However, the redownload buffer is observable in that an attacker can probably disconnect mid-redownload, and see how much you accepted afterwards.

I'll run some numbers to see how quickly these parameters change and suggest some quantization or noise.

It looks like the output parameters only change roughly every 22 days. I don't think quantizing further gains us much, especially as the attack only applies during IBD, so peers generally already know you just started.

nit: feel free to ignore, just mentioning what gave me pause when i was reading from scratch.

That last sentence in the comment threw me off a little bit. `future_limit` is a number of headers, weighted by the exponentially-decreasing contribution each batch makes. The last sentence could be read as it representing a single batch, while really it represents *all* batches, so the check later can be essentially "if the contribution of the entire tail of headers at the current probability is no more than a rounding error, we are done".

> [b819b05](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35642/changes/b819b057075bd682fab763be76a73e15123e3826) _headerssync: add computation of optimal sync parameters_:

I wonder whether we need to find the optimum this precisely. If we restricted the buffer to whole commitment periods, we could calculate its size directly, and a logarithmic estimate might replace the period search too. The earlier experiments suggest a small memory increase could let us remove both searches. Do you think that tradeoff is worth exploring?

<details>
<summary>Whole-period calculation and earlier measurements</summary>

AI summary:
> For whole-period buffers (`M = 0`), the attack rate reduces to `2^-K * (1.5*P - 0.5)`. Choosing at least one check and `K = ceil(log2(1.5*P / attack_headers))` meets the budget without searching for the buffer. A corrected logarithmic estimate for the period also removed the other search in the earlier experiments. Across the existing 50 vectors, that used about 1.1% more memory on average, with a maximum increase of 3.9%. Those are observed differences, not a bound for every input. The original exact outputs would remain the comparison baseline.
</details>
